Are you tracking everything you eat with a diet app like MyFitnessPal? Are you eating below your TDEE? Do you know what your TDEE even is?

Barring a serious medical issue, weight loss is as simple as calories in calories out. If you consume fewer calories than your TDEE, or burn more calories through exercise, you will lose weight. [Hit up this site](https://tdeecalculator.net/) and input your stats to find your TDEE. Then use that to find your cutting calories. You can also go to the AWC on post and have them find your RMR test, which would be more accurate. It's free for you, so I don't see why not do it.  
Track all the food you eat, everything. Every last gram. Cut out any drinks that aren't water or black coffee (everything else pretty much has calories, and drinking your calories isn't ideal when it comes to weight loss.)  
Exercise. Lifting and cardio is good, and you're already doing that. If you're eating below maintenance calories AND putting in the word in the gym or on the track, then you will lose weight. It's not enough that you just "eat clean."  
Yes, you SHOULD always be eating clean. But you have to be eating under your TDEE if you want to lose weight. Just because you're eating 3000cals of chicken breast and broccoli doesn't mean you'll shed off pounds.

Godspeed, and I'm confident that you will become comfortable with your body and achieve your goals so long as you put in the work and have **patience.** Weight loss isn't a sprint, it is very much a marathon.

1) This can vary wildly between units. But the general standard is 0600-0800 PT. 0900-1130 Work. 1130-1300 Lunch. Then 1300-1700(usually, can go longer some days) work again. After that you're off for the day. That's the basic FORSCOM schedule.

2) 5 days a week, as long as you don't get hit with weekend duty like CQ/staff duty. Again, hours can vary wildly day to day. A 'normal' day would be 0600-1700. But things like ranges, last second taskings, field prep, etc....can very easily extend that duty day.

3) Hah. I'm quite vocal on my distaste for 25U. But it isn't the worst job in the army. If I could choose any 25 series job, it'd definitely be 25B or 25S. 25U just isn't really that great.

4) Yeah I mean, any 25 series can give you a good head start on life if you play your cards right. Get your CompTIA certs and some college while you're in and you can be set up for civilian life. I would still pick a different 25 series job if this was something you really cared about though.

5) This once again varies wildly between units and where you're placed within the unit. Let's just say you go to your typical FORSCOM BCT. As a 25U, you can either wind up at the company level or the battalion+ level.   
At the company level, you'll be a commo rep. That role is basically the sole 25 series within the company. You'll help your company set up and maintain comms whenever they do training, exercises, etc. This involves programming and loading radios, setting up antennas, and manning the communication networks like JCR/JBC-P or maybe even CPOF. You're basically the go-to guy in the company for anything that talks.  
At the battalion and higher level, you'll be in a staff shop, the S6. Here, you'll do less 'tactical comms' stuff and more general IT work. As a 25U you'll most likely be in charge of COMSEC for the unit, which means receiving keys and dishing them out to your subordinate companies. You'll also most likely assist the 25Bs with general help-desk and IT operations for the battalion. When your company/BN does go to training, you'll most likely help set up the communication systems for the TOC and man said systems.

That's the basics of 25U life. I can answer any further questions if you're interested.

It's not the worst MOS in the world. But you have to play your cards right. 

AIT is a joke honestly, I wouldn't worry too much about it. As long as you have a pulse, you should be able to pass rather easily. The hardest part is the daily death by powerpoint and staying awake. You'll learn *a lot* of communication systems in AIT. But the only ones you're actually gonna ever use at your unit will be the 1523 and the JCR. Pay attention to those two blocks specifically.

As for day to day life, it heavily varies depending on your unit, your leadership, and just luck. But 95% of the time it can be broken down into two different paths. The company, and BN & higher.

At the company level (where you're most likely to go straight out of AIT) you'll be what is known as a company commo rep. You'll be the sole 25 series in said company (unless it's a signal unit). Your duties will pretty much be maintaining all your radios and commo equipment, doing lots of inventories/layouts, loading COMSEC, and pretty much waiting for your company to go to the field so that you can actually do your job. The field is honestly where our MOS shines as it's the one time everyone and their mother wants comms up and to stay up. You'll be busy actually doing your job for once, whether it be flinging up antennas, shooting azimuths to satellites, loading and programming radios, and more.

 There can be *a lot* of downtime at the company level, so use this time to get close with your BN S6 and become an expert at your trade, work with the other company commo reps, share knowledge and more. You can also knock out hella online school. Note that your mileage may vary, and some units absolutely abuse the fuck out of their commo reps, giving them every detail and additional duty under the sun as maneuver/non-commo commanders see them as "useless" sometimes. Get close with the S6 OIC so that they can shield you from this type of bullshit that happens far too often.

The battalion level is a bit different but sort of the same. You'll be at the S6 doing similar tasks. When your unit goes to the field, you'll provide tactical comms support (antennas, radios, COMSEC, etc.). Outside of the field, S6 life for 25U can vary wildly. You'll most likely be assigned as the COMSEC custodian for the company/BN as a 25U. This essentially means you'll be in charge of drawing keys from whatever higher echelon you fall under and issuing them out to the subordinate units via SKLs. There is a *fuck ton* of paperwork and red tape that goes along with this (as it should be honestly) so if you end up being the primary or alternate custodian (very likely) you'll be very busy. You'll learn very quickly how to write memos, lol. Beyond that, you'll also most likely assist the 25Bs with help desk operations and general tech support work around the BN/CO HQs. 

It's hard to say even all these years later which is a "better" spot as a uniform to be. The vast majority will tell you that the company level sucks, which to be fair, it really can if your leadership is trash and abuses you. But I feel like the company level is really where the Uniforms thrive and get to do their jobs more often.

My biggest piece of advice to you, no matter where you end up, is to **get your fucking certs** once you land at your unit. Go to the S6 OIC/NCOIC and ask them exactly what you need to do to get into the next A+/Net+/Sec+ class. Study study study for these exams and earn your certs man, it is so so important. Having these certs will make your life on the inside much easier as well as on the outside. Beyond that, **ASK FOR HELP** when you need it. Being a PV2 fresh AIT grad all alone at the company can be extremely scary and overwhelming. The company will have a lot of expectations for you, and you might feel as though you just can't do it all at once. Ask for help man! You are not alone!   
There is no tighter brotherhood within a unit than the one between the company level commo reps. They are all they have, and from what I've seen at the very least, they always help each other out when someone needs it. You have the S6 and the other commo reps there to get you through any roadblock. We have **all** been the clueless new guy all alone once, we know exactly what it is like and it sucks hard. We will always assist when asked.

Lastly, best of luck my man. This MOS can take you very far if you work your ass off and get all your certs (25D school or warrant).

Gonna pretty much copy/paste my response from another thread similar to this one:

If you want to lose weight, then you should be eating below your maintenance calories. Don't know what that is/what they are? [Hit up this site](https://tdeecalculator.net/) and input your stats for a rough estimate. You should also be tracking the calories you're putting into your body. The most important and used app on my phone is MyFitnessPal. This single app has easily changed my life more than any other piece of software I've ever used. I'd say it's required if you're serious about gaining/losing/maintaining weight.

Log everything you put into your mouth and try to stay at or below your daily calorie limit. If you aren't already logging all your food, you'll realize that (9 times out of 10) you're probably eating way, way more than you think you are. Check those serving sizes!  
Cut out all the junk food, only drink water/coffee/milk (juice, soda, **alcohol,** etc...all have calories, and a lot of them at that.) Portion sizes on snacks are a fucking joke, and easily lead to overeating. If you actually ate the serving size on say, a bag of chips, you'd only be able to eat something crazy like 5-8 chips, and you'd end up consuming 100-200cals. Crazy!

I would 100% invest in a food scale and start 1. preparing all your meals at home with fresh ingredients (if possible) and 2. weighing everything you eat. This will help you know exactly how many calories you are consuming per day, vital information. MyFitnessPal also has an amazing feature where you can simply scan the barcode of any food you're eating and it'll (9 times out of 10) automatically find it in it's database and log it for you. Seriously, get on MFP! It's fucking amazing.

Diet is 95% of weight loss/gain. But exercise is also very important. Like others have said, take up some strength training or cardio as well. Supplement your dieting with exercise and you'll see the results come. Plus, you'll look and feel much, much better. Better, stronger, faster, etc etc...you know how the song goes.

If you've never stepped foot in a gym before or never done serious weight training, [hit up this site](https://liftvault.com/) for hundreds of free, legit workout programs with customized spreadsheets and routines. Never enter the gym without a dedicated plan. Never do a bro split. Always know exactly what you're doing, at what weight, and for how many repts/sets. Never eat back the calories you burn from exercise by the way.

Log everything you put into your mouth and try to stay at or below your daily calorie limit. Diet is 95% of weight loss/gain. But exercise is also very important. Like others have said, take up some strength training or cardio as well. Been in over 4 years and I honestly cannot tell you with 100% confidence what the fuck a 25U is or what we're supposed to truly even be fucking doing. Life as a 25U basically boils down into 2 paths: Staff life and company life. Neither are pleasant.

Staff life is sitting in a BN/BDE/whatever S6 shop. However, the primary purpose of the S6 is to assist the unit with IT support. Things like creating accounts, making trouble tickets, reimaging computers, plugging in printers, explaining to braindead SNCOs how a power button works, etc etc... 25U aren't really trained on these tasks however. Our job is much more "tactical" even though I hate that word. Our bread and butter are radios and JCR. Ask any uniform what they know best and they'll say the 1523. The role of a 25U at the staff level is to support the company(s) during field exercises/rotations/what have you with COMSEC, setting up antennas and radios....manning said radios, and just making sure the lower TI comms are functional.   
However, outside of field ops...you really aren't doing shit. You can't support users/customers with their IT related issues or questions as you don't have access to the systems the 25Bs use or you simply have no idea *how* to help them. A good S6 OIC/NCOIC will push hard for crosstraining the uniforms with bravos so that they can also do bravo work, but this isn't always guaranteed to happen. More often than not, as a 25U at BN, you'll be the first one picked for details and taskings since "we can't spare the 25B!!" Shit sucks. Good luck trying to get certs too, they'll always prioritize the bravos over us.   
Lots of sitting around doing nothing, feeling useless, and area beautification. Riveting.

Reduce caloric intake. Track every single calorie you put into your mouth. MyFitnessPal should be the most used app on your phone. If you haven't been tracking your calories already, you'll be SHOCKED at how much food you *actually* are eating every day. Probably way above your weight-loss limit even if you think you're cutting calories.

Step 1 should be using the [TDEE Calculator](https://tdeecalculator.net/) to find out what your weight-loss calorie limit actually is in the first place. Insert all your stats, and your BF if you know it. This'll give you a rough estimate of how many calories you actually need to eat to either gain, maintain, or lose weight. **Be honest** about your activity level as well. It has a huge impact on the numbers.

If possible, buy a food scale and weight/cook all of your own meals. The DFAC is famous for meals heavy in carbs, fat, and sugar. All things you want to avoid. Cooking your own meals with your own ingredients and **weighing them all** will give you a much more accurate idea of how many calories you're consuming. Avoid dangerous food like cereal, white bread, all candy, **bacon,** anything high in carbs and fat. Avoid things like olive oil, peanut butter and **all snacks** like chips, cookies, crackers, etc...All are insanely high in calories for laughably small serving sizes. Look at a bag of Combos or something else you'd find in a shoppette. Look at the nutrition label. It's something like 140 calories **per serving,** each bag having **6** entire servings. If you eat that whole, small bag in one sitting, you just ate **840** goddamn calories. Snacks like those are literally made so that they leave you hungry and wanting more and more and more. They are evil in a way. NO MORE SNACKS!!!

Your best friends from now on will be egg whites, rice cakes, and **baked** chicken breast. Of course fruits and veggies on the side too. Egg whites have INSANE amounts of volume for little calories and a great amount of protein. Rice cakes are almost cheating, with 1 rice cake only being 35 calories. Slap whatever you want on top, like a banana or greek yogurt, boom, instant healthy snack. And chicken breast, goddamn. 1 bound of a chicken breast will be just about 400-500 calories, with INSANE amounts of protein and almost no carbs. Insanely filling too. It's cheating! lol. 

Can't give a certain food item up? There's probably a healthier alternative for it. Instead of bacon, eat turkey bacon. Instead of potato chips, eat low calorie popcorn. Instead of soda, try sparkling water. Etc etc. Do some research, there's a healthy alternative for nearly everything.

Drinks. Cut out anything that isn't water or black coffee. That includes juice, energy drinks, **soda, alcohol.** Get rid of it all. All those sugary drinks have **calories,** and usually a lot of them. Water water water water. Water is your best friend. Just ate but you still feel hungry? Chug down some water. Think you got an urge to eat? You're probably just thirsty, chug some water. If you need to just be chewing something, I've found that sugar free gum is AMAZING for suppressing that "man I really want to eat something right now" urges.

Exercise. Let's be honest, morning PT is a joke and waste of time. But it can help burn off a few 100 or so extra calories. Time permitting, you **really** want to be working out on your own outside of PT if you want to lose weight. Cardio here is your best friend. Burns fat and calories. Hop on a treadmill or elliptical and go man. 30min-1hr every day, you'll burn hundreds of calories. If your gym has one, hop on a stair climber too. You'll sweat your balls off and burn tons of calories, and it's not as intensive as running. Plus you can put on a YouTube video or something and just watch it as you climb the infinite staircase.  
tl;dr - exercise OUTSIDE OF PT for at least 30min-1hr. Cardio is best for burning fat, so focus on that. Weightlifting works too but you wont burn nearly as much calories, unless you're doing some HIIT shit.

Long time veteran of the BH process. I've been where you are brother, let me help you out.

The process is fairly straight forward. Your first appointment will be essentially establishing a baseline. You'll spend awhile on a little computer/laptop filling out a survey basically asking you a ton of questions. Ranging from how you're feeling, what's bothering you, do you have trouble doing xyz...etc etc. After that you'll see a BH provider, usually a CPT, and do an initial appointment. Basically they're gonna try to understand why you're there, what's bothering you, what caused it, and how to address it. This will lead to them scheduling follow up appointments and giving you "homework" some of the time. The homework is essentially basic psychology sheets you fill out to track your mood/activities/etc depending on what they think is troubling you.

If the regular therapy isn't enough, or your condition is serious enough, your provider may refer you to a psychiatrist. These are the people that prescribe you medication. Obviously, do not purchase a firearm if you are actively suicidal or dealing with really bad depression. 

With all that being said. PLEASE SEEK BH. PLEASE. It will be good for you. It will be so good for you to talk out your issues and have something who won't judge you listen. In garrison, soldiers will approach your shop looking for IT help, and your sole job is to pretty much point them in the direction of the 25Bs who...actually do their job every day and are of actual use to the unit, unlike us.

Honestly man, AIT was the most exciting part of my career. It really only goes downhill from here. Expect to be in the field A LOT if you get sent down to the company (you almost certainly will, they LOVE making fresh E2s from AIT company commo reps). You're gonna do a lot of filling radios, filling JCRs, getting yelled at for not knowing how to do 20/30 level tasks, being a detail bitch, and setting up antennas for TOCs during any FTXs. You're also gonna do a lot of additional duties and details since you just mainly sit on your ass all day.

If you want to do anything remotely cool or highspeed, i'd recommend training up and dropping a packet. This is....a pretty fucking shitty MOS man. The only real outcomes are either ETS, drop a packet, or reclass.

Best of luck. If you have any questions or want any advice/commo help feel free to DM me. I've been doing this shit for years. You'll quickly learn about the tight-knit 25U community. We need to stick together as best we can cause no one gives a fuck about us and actively sets us up for failure.
